newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shareholder group opposes shortening AGMs.
newsitem.headline: German shareholder group opposes shortening AGMs.

text.p: The German group for the protection of shareholders' interests (DSW) said on Wednesday that any attempts to shorten often notoriously long German shareholders meetings went against the spirit of the meetings.

The length of shareholders meetings, which can sometimes drag on for up to 20 hours, is a contentious issue for German companies which want to curtail meetings by introducing an order of business which would put a limit on discussion time.
President of the DSW, Otto Graf Lambsdorff agreed that many meetings were very long and that some shareholders abused their right to speak at the meetings, using question time to delay proceedings.
"There are shareholders who abuse the right to speak at the shareholders meetings," Lambsdorff said at a DSW news conference.

"However, the other side of the argument is that these annual meetings are the only chance shareholders get a chance to air their views and they should have the right to air their views," said Lambsdorff.
Lambsdorff said that there were possible legal barriers to shortening the meetings and that many long meetings needed to be that long.
The DSW went on to say that it welcomes moves to make German accounts more transparent, but said a suitable accounting system was necessary.

Moves have been afoot in recent times to introduce the Generally Agreed Accounting Principles (GAAP) accounting system or the International Accounting System (IAS) into Germany, where accounting practices can often baffle investors.
"American law contains legislation which German law does not have, which means GAAP might not be quite right for Germany," said Hans Peter Schreib, managing director of DSW.
Schreib said he was more positive on the possibilities on the development of IAS, but that the conditions for introducing IAS were not yet fully in place.
Another important issue for the DSW was how quoted companies would approach shifting their business from the deutschemark to the euro when currency union, planned for January 1 1999, arrived.
Asked about the prospects for the punctual introduction of the euro, Lambsdorff said that he thought currency union would take place on time, but that there were issues still to be addressed.
These include seeing just how wide the scope for interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for currency union membership would be.
